doc.title: Longineu Parsons interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 17, 2026

title: Playing outside the chord and tension in composition
summary: Parsons says a note outside the chord depends on intent and context; for a modern composer there are twelve tones and no outside, only devices for building tension.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: If you have a student trumpet player working on improvisation and they constantly are playing – well let’s say an F sharp over a B flat chord. Is there a difference between playing outside the chord if you do it on purpose or if you’re not aware that you’re doing it?

Okay outside the chord. Well if it’s a B flat what, let’s say if it’s a B flat seventh chord and you play an F sharp then you’re playing, okay we could say that’s flat sixth or flat thirteen. So where is that outside of the chord?
I had a feeling you were going to say that.
But there is a difference if you know what you’re doing and if you don’t.

Yeah, how can you tell with a student? I guess I’m thinking back on when, especially with junior high kids, trying to teach them to improvise and they keep playing a note that is a little bit advanced from them and I don’t feel that they know – right?
Oh yeah. That’s a wrong note then.
In that case it’s a wrong note I guess.

Yeah, yeah. Everything in context. But for me as a composer, these things, there are twelve tones in every octave. And so what we think of in classic theory is right notes and wrong notes, we think about devices – as modern composers we think about these things as devices for raising the tension of the music. But there are twelve tones in every octave. So you might have to start raising – maybe you want it nice and calm so you’re only going to use chord tones for a moment. But then you start using maybe extensions as it rises, but then maybe you need a good flat nine in there when it gets to a certain point, you know when it goes, you know when you’re taking it up you need these things to develop your arc of your music. If you look at classical compositions most of the time there’s an arc. It goes back to the Fibonacci numbers and all that. And so how are you going to construct your arc or whatever you’re going to do with it musically. And it’s these notes, these other – these notes that are not the regular chord tones that have a lot to do with it. I mean as we rise and we get the energy up we may need this big cluster where we [scats] and I mean a great example is film music you know where you have to express what’s going on on screen. You’re going to voice things a certain way if it’s a gentle scene where two people are speaking with each other gently who love each other or

whatever or something you know, something nice. And they you will use different things say if you have somebody holding a pistol on somebody. You’re going to need more tension in that music. So notes are going to be closer together, they’re going to be notes that are not necessarily what we think of as chord tones. But some people would say they’re outside but they’re actually, as a modern composer, there’s no outside.
